There are more than 40 varieties of ticks in Canada , and many are known to carry lyme . The species that are of the biggest concern are the blacklegged tick in Eastern Canada and the western blacklegged tick in B.C. <p> While early signs of the disease can be fairly mild , including fever , fatigue , swollen lymph nodes and a bullseye-shaped rash near the location of the bite , later stages can cause severe headaches , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ joints , difficulties with thinking and memory and facial paralysis , among other symptoms . <p> First tracked nationally in 2009 , reported cases of lyme disease have risen greatly in the past quarter-century , to more than 5,000 in last year 's preliminary data from just a few hundred per year in the early 2010s . <p> " In Canada , there were only a handful of cases only a decade ago , " Millien said . " It 's not a linear relationship , it 's exponential when a disease emerges . So it 's going to get bigger and bigger , and in an exponential way . That 's the expectation . " <p> PHAC notes that cases are often underreported because they go undetected , possibly even to those infected with the disease . Case counts can vary annually due to underlying weather , trends in outdoor activity among humans and prevention efforts by public health authorities , they say . <p> Anyone who develops symptoms after a tick bite , or does after visitinga high-risk area for tick-borne lyme , is advised to contact their @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ after exposure , posing the best chance of recovery , though symptoms may persist after treatment is complete , PHAC says . <h> How to remove a tick <p> George Chaconas is a professor at the University of Calgary 's Cumming School of Medicine who studies the bacteria that causes lyme disease . <p> " If you 're in an area known to have ticks , protect yourself , " he told CTVNews.ca by phone . " Wear light-coloured clothing , so if you pick up a tick , you can see it . Tuck your pants into your socks . You may look a little bit funny , but if you do that , if a tick gets on your foot and crawls upwards , which is what they do , it 's not going to get under your pants and crawl up to your groin or somewhere else . " <p> Insect repellants can also help . If bitten , Chaconas says it 's important to quickly but carefully remove a tick by the head without squeezing its body . @@125359742 <p> My wife and I arrived in Barrie in the autumn of 1988 , after living and working abroad for many years . <p> Although we are Canadian , our return was a bit of a shock . <p> One of the first things that struck me was the volume of garbage generated every week by a typical Barrie household . In England , we ( two adults , plus two young daughters ) produced less than 30 litres of garbage . <p> In Barrie , we continued to put out a similar amount . <p> But others discarded far more . <p> Across the street , our neighbours , a family with three children , filled five large black bags every week . Even the retired couple next door put out two bags . <p> My initial reaction was mild horror . Several months after arriving here , I became a founding member of a group concerned with the environment . My talk may have spurred our group to begin recycling . Apart from a very few Ontario communities , recycling was n't yet a " thing . " <p> Barrie only collected paper and cardboard . We set up to collect plastics monthly in the parking lot on Mulcaster Street , across Collier Street from city hall . <p> We inspected the plastics to ensure they were clean ( " please bring them back washed " ) and separated them into huge clear bags . <p> By late afternoon , we loaded them into a 16-tonne truck borrowed from my then-employer , Comet Chemical Company . I then drove the load to a company in Lindsay , which used it to make plastic lumber . They loved our " clean " plastics , and stayed open on Saturday just to receive it . <p> We incorporated in 1991 as Environmental Action Barrie , a registered charity ( now Living Green Barrie ) . By then , we had installed 10,000 low-flush volume toilets ( now mandatory ) , low-flow showers , taps , hot water tank-insulating " blankets " and draft proofing . Energuide for Houses was recently revived by Natural Resources Canada with evaluation by a government-registered energy adviser . <p> Returning to trash , places that could be used as garbage dumps -- politely , " landfills " -- are hard to find . @@125383930 <p> Everyone who wants a good future for their children in light of climate change should learn to understand the difference between an ecologist , a naturalist , a scientist , a landscape architect , an arborist , and a forester . <p> Each is trained to look at situations in a different light . For example , every municipal government should have an urban ecologist on staff , not an arborist or forester . I first looked at situations as a naturalist , but now I find myself assessing each situation as an ecologist . <p> Natural history is a domain of inquiry involving organisms , including animals , fungi , and plants , in their natural environment , leaning more toward observational than experimental methods of study . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> A person who studies natural history is called a naturalist or natural historian . The study of natural history dates back to Pliny the Elder , who published the encyclopedia of natural history from 77 to 79 A.D. <p> Natural history became the third branch of academic knowledge during the Renaissance along with what we @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and geological sciences . During its heyday in the 17th century , many famous gentleman scientists made contributions to the field . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Carl Linnaeus ( 1707-1778 ) formalized binomial nomenclature with his first edition of " Systema Naturae , " first printed in 1735 , to the 10th edition in 1758 . Three of the greatest English naturalists of the 19th century started to make new discoveries around the world . Henry Walter Bates ( 1825-1892 ) , Alfred Russel Wallace ( 1823-1913 ) , and Charles Darwin ( 1809-1882 ) all made amazing discoveries as naturalists , and Darwin , with his theory of evolution later as an ecologist . <p> I first read " The Naturalist on the River Amazons " by Bates years ago before I started to lead nature tours on the Amazon River , and knew from that point that I wanted to be a naturalist . They transformed biology from a descriptive to a theory-based science . I could include Richard Spruce ( 1817-1893 ) in that group as well . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> I then discovered @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ organism and not as a mechanism . I wanted to study the interactions between living things and their environment using modelling and data analysis . <p> Five warbler species and the niches they use in a black spruce tree from Robert H. MacArthur 's 1958 ecology paper . <p> Bob Bowles <p> However , the greatest ecologist ever was Robert H. MacArthur ( 1930-1972 ) , a Canadian-born American ecologist who made a major impact on many areas of community and population ecology . After a bachelor 's degree and master 's degree in mathematics , he switched to ecology for his PhD at Yale University and wrote his first ecology paper on " Fluctuations of Animal Populations and a Measure of Community Stability " in 1955 . <p> MacArthur changed the ecology world with his famous 1958 research paper on the five warbler species foraging in black @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Park in the State of Maine behind the Bass Harbor Lighthouse , close to the Canadian border . <p> The warbler species in the study were Cape May , blackburnian , black-throated green , bay-breasted , and yellow-rumped ( myrtle ) warblers , but I have read many accounts where the wrong warbler species were listed by the authors . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> If you have ever tried to follow a small warbler species as it moves in and around spruce boughs , you would realize how difficult it would be to follow five different species foraging in the same trees . He used his mathematical background and divided the tree into different sections . <p> Five warbler species feeding in the same tree would be an exception to the ecological rule of competitive exclusion that states that no two species with essentially the same niche can coexist , that one species will always out compete and displace the other . <p> MacArthur was able to observe that each species used a different part of the tree for foraging . Cape May preferred the branch tips at the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of tree , bay-breasted in middle outer branches , black-throated green in the dense branches in the middle , and yellow-rumped in the lower trunk and branches . <p> MacArthur 's paper marked a major turning point in how the science of ecology was conducted . He used something that most scientific research does today : hypotheses tested with statistics . MacArthur must have been an amazing ecologist . It is unfortunate that he died so young . <p> A.M. @@125389949 <h> Key points <p> Anyone can benefit from a deeper dive into their own relationship with nature . <p> I met Dr. Elizabeth Haase via the Group for the Advancement of Psychiatry , with her leadership on the Climate Committee overlapping with my committee on Disasters , Trauma , and Global Health . Struck by her deep love of nature , humanity , healing , and psychiatric excellence , I was overjoyed when she offered me her new book , the Handbook of Climate Psychiatry and Psychotherapy : A Manual for Clinicians , during the annual American Psychiatric Association meeting in Los Angeles . Amidst a strange world of self-driving cars and robot delivery bots holding up traffic , sprawling miles of low-lying cityscape , the mighty waves of the Pacific , and heated air , while touring areas stricken by wildfires and alternatively chilling with colleagues in Venice Beach and Beverly Hills , I could n't help but be struck by the tension between nature and civilization . <p> Autographed copy in hand , I devoured the book on the flight back from LA . While sections are impressive @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is relatable to a broader audience . There is an array of soulful and profound observations , pragmatic suggestions , and the incontrovertible mark of someone who has spent a lifetime in contemplation of what most truly connects us with who and what we are . I hope you enjoy our brief interview , and take some time to explore Dr. Haase 's impressive contributions . <p> GHB : What topics are part of climate psychotherapy and psychiatry ? <p> EH : You can think of climate psychiatry and psychology as all the factors associated with mental health and well-being that are influenced by climate change . We often break these down into a few large categories . This includes neurobiological effects , like the changes in brain function with high temperature or new or increased neuroinfectious diseases , psychological effects , like grief for losses in the natural world , and ways that climate change is a " threat multiplier " for other unequal social conditions that negatively affect health such as air pollution and urban heat island effects . I also think it is critical to include cognitive @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reactionary thinking increases with climate change in order to effect the best response . <p> GHB : How do you think about the environment and nature ? What is important about the environment and nature for our mental health ? <p> EH : Nature for me is everything -- awe , solace , inspiration , nurturance . I am not alone , though . Many people will tell you their most powerful experiences of stillness , beauty , and wonder occurred in nature . Scientific studies show that time in nature is really good for our immune system , diabetes , hypertension , pulmonary disease , attention and emotional health , among many other benefits . Time in nature decreases loneliness and rumination and improves joy , self esteem , and social connectedness . Interactions with animals help people with anxiety disorders , autism , and health problems . I have a lot of patients who have reduced or eliminated medications after getting an animal . <p> GHB : What impacts does climate change have on well-being ? <p> EH : Climate change impacts all of the lifestyle pillars of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Good quality food is harder to come by with drought and flooding . Heat , disasters , and changes like sea level rise will increase all kinds of social stress : forced migration , increased civic violence , more exposure to toxins , poor sleep , and so on . Some argue that there will be gains from tourism , outdoor activity , and less cold-related illness from more warm weather , but studies show that these gains are more than offset by negative health and economic effects . <p> GHB:How can psychotherapy help folks affected by climate change ? <p> EH : Most people working in this area feel that group therapy approaches are most empowering for people who are distressed about climate change . It takes a village to tackle these problems . Climate cafes are an easily organized way of gathering people together for a structured conversation about the climate concerns people have and the hurdles they face in themselves and their communities to get to a sustainable way of living . For people who want to go deeper , I recommend the Work that Reconnects @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ value-based reflection , your relationship with the more-than-human world , and what you can connect to and let go of so that your lifestyle comes into better alignment with your climate response . Fossil fuels have given us such an amazing power to live as we wish . But it can feel good to disconnect from constant marketing pulls to do , have , and be more , and we have all the tools to continue our lifestyle through clean energy sources . <p> In terms of individual therapy , anyone can benefit from a deeper dive into their own relationship with nature and the existential planetary emergency we are in . In the book , I offer a comprehensive assessment therapists and individuals can do to examine all of the aspects of personal psychology that are relevant to climate change . I also give therapy techniques for experimenting with new kinds of hope , future imagining , and shaking off the disavowal and dialectic extremes that can lead to climate despair . <p> It 's also important to remember , though , that almost everyone is concerned about climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and so really any conversation about environmental changes and reducing fossil fuel use is going to be helpful . For a lot of people , change feels overwhelming , and just talking with your neighbor can help them and you get over the hurdle , rather than everyone needing formal psychotherapy . I find a 50 percent rule helps my anxiety . You only need to make a 30 to 50 percent change : fly about half as often , or connect up your work and vacation trips . Throw away half as much food and eat half as much meat . Have two children instead of four -- that kind of thing . <p> GHB : What are some key resources for people who want to learn more about how they can make a difference ? <p> EH : Al Gore 's Climate Reality Project offers a wonderful free training so anyone can get knowledgeable and figure out how they can use their own unique abilities and interests to make a difference . @@125390040 <p> I just graduated with a Master 's of Liberal Arts , where I used critical race theory ( CRT ) as a framework for understanding climate change and its impacts on communities . That 's a mouthful , I know . But this also represents a degree I fought for -- through late nights , towering stacks of books , and a growing sense that the world can be a more sustainable and equitable place for all . <p> CRT has become one of this country 's favorite villains -- splashed across the front pages of newspapers , hurled like a slur by politicians , and blamed for everything from school board fights to the supposed unraveling of America . <p> But here 's the wildest part : despite all the shouting and panic about CRT , almost nobody who is disparaging it can actually tell you what it is . <p> Advertisement <p> So let 's get this straight : Critical race theory is n't some secret curriculum thrust upon grade school students . Developed in the late 1970s and early ' 80s by academics , it 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and more through the lens of race . It 's used at the college or graduate school level -- if one 's lucky to have professors who dare to ask challenging questions . <p> CRT asks why some neighborhoods get parks and others get landfills . Why disaster relief comes quickly to certain zip codes and drags its heels in others . Why , after generations , do the same communities keep getting hit hardest by COVID-19 , climate change , and every other new crisis ? <p> Advertisement <p> Laws , policies , and institutions -- even if everyone involved in shaping them thinks they 're being fair -- are put under a microscope by critical race theorists . That 's because even with the best intentions , systems can still end up treating some groups of people better than others and making life harder for others , often in ways that are challenging to see unless you really look for them . And without critical race theorists , it 's likely we 'd have fewer people uncovering this veil that undoubtedly produces unequal lived experiences for non-white people @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Charles Orgbon <p> CRT provides us with the language and history to connect the dots -- and the hope that if we see the system for what it is , we can actually make it better . Guided by this vision , I 'm not interested in some abstract theory , but the lived reality of who wins and loses in America -- and why . CRT gives us tools for tracing those lines . It 's not about blaming anyone for things they personally did or did n't do . It 's about refusing to accept " that 's just the way it is " as an answer . <p> Still , almost every time someone hears about my degree , I get the same knee-jerk reactions , especially , " Is n't that the thing that teaches kids to feel bad about being white ? " and " Are n't you just saying everything is about race ? " <p> Advertisement <p> I 've heard these two misconceptions -- and many others -- from strangers in line at Domino 's , from old friends , from people @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- including Donald Trump -- have spent the last decade turning CRT into a boogeyman , right alongside LGBTQ history , both of which they want to use to scare school boards and corporations into erasing any perspective that is n't straight , white , and cisgender . They want you to think CRT is a threat . They want you to be afraid . <p> But let 's be honest : these attacks are n't just about misunderstanding -- they 're about power . The people leading this crusade do n't want us asking tough questions about who gets what . They do n't want to discuss the policies -- written and unwritten -- that skew things in one direction . They call CRT " anti-American , " but what they 're saying is do n't look too closely , do n't question the rules , and do n't demand change . <p> That 's why CRT matters . If we ca n't ask why climate change is devastating certain communities more than others , or why once redlined neighborhoods are now the hottest places in our cities , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ? It 's not about shame . It 's about honesty and the belief that honesty leads to action . <p> Advertisement <p> And , yes , it is racist to try to shut down these conversations . It 's racist to erase the experiences of Black , brown , queer , and other marginalized people from our classrooms and our laws . The same movement that wants to ban CRT wants to silence any group that complicates their version of America . <p> The author is pictured receiving his diploma on graduation day . <p> Courtesy of Charles Orgbon <p> I wo n't pretend it 's easy to " out " myself as having studied critical race theory . Universities are backing away from the theory , programs that utilize it are disappearing , and I genuinely wonder if I 'll be one of the last people to graduate with a degree in CRT . It 's no longer hypothetical that a university could be forced to bow to an American president 's desire to shape what is taught in academic institutions -- but that just makes this work @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ n't get this degree to hide . I plan to use it to ask hard questions , to work for policies rooted in justice , and to help communities demand more than the bare minimum . Whether I 'm working in business , public policy , education , or environmental justice , I want to ensure that the problems we 're all living with are acknowledged for what they are and get addressed . <p> If you 've been told to fear CRT , I get it , but that 's what those in power would want you to feel . The real danger , however , is a country where we 're too scared to ask why things are the way they are , or to imagine something better . <p> CRT is n't a threat to America . It 's a chance for America to live up to its promises for all its citizens . The only people who should be afraid are those desperate to prevent inequitable outcomes from playing out over and over again . <p> Advertisement <p> We do n't have to settle for silence @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ can challenge , and we can change . Through loans , underwriting services and investments , banks pour billions of dollars into oil , gas and coal companies every year , financing the construction of pipelines and investing in shares of mining companies that enable the continued extraction and burning of carbon-heavy fuels . <p> These activities are invisible to the average customer . Most people do n't realize that the money they deposit does n't simply sit in a vault ; it 's used by the bank to make more money , often by lending to large corporations , including fossil fuel companies . <p> The oil and gas industry often requires massive amounts of upfront capital to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ infrastructure like pipelines and refineries . Pension funds , whether through employer-sponsored plans , personal RRSPs , or even the Canada Pension Plan , frequently invest in fossil fuel companies . These stocks have long been seen as blue-chip investments , valued for their stability and returns . That view is becoming outdated with climate change increasingly being seen as a financial risk . <p> What has not changed , though , is the massive investment by banks that have supported fossil fuel companies for decades . @@125425716 <h> Vancouver Park Board invites residents to adopt a tree <p> WITH a warmer than average June and July forecasted for Vancouver , the Vancouver Park Board is encouraging residents to adopt young street trees in their neighbourhood and keep it watered . The Adopt-a-Tree program supports the establishment of young trees that are less than five years old as Vancouver works to grow the area of its tree canopy by 30% by 2050 . <p> " Trees are Vancouver 's hardest-working infrastructure , " says Vancouver Park Board Chair , Laura Christensen . " They provide shade and cooling during heat and slow the flow of rainfall into storm drains to prevent flooding . They also clean our air , support wildlife and make Vancouver more livable . If we want trees to take care of us , we need to take care of them . " <p> During watering restrictions trees can be hand watered anytime or between 5 a.m. and 9 a.m. any day of the week if using a sprinkler . To sign up , visit **25;3458;TOOLONG and view an interactive map with trees available for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ how to care for your tree . In-person sign-up opportunities will also be available through June . Watering bags will be provided to new adopters while supplies last . <p> " Extra watering for young trees will contribute to a stronger , healthier urban forest , " says Amit Gandha , Director of Parks . " During the hotter and drier months our crews are watering trees throughout the city . However , young trees in particular need some extra help as they do n't have the big root systems of older trees and require more water while they try to establish . Ensuring the success of our newly planted trees is vital as we work to increase our tree canopy , particularly in neighbourhoods like Strathcona , Sunset and the Downtown core . " <p> Vancouver has made strong progress in growing its canopy , with current city-wide coverage at 25% -- a four per cent increase since 2013 . Achieving 30% canopy coverage is ambitious , but achievable for Metro Vancouver 's most developed and densely populated city , says the Park Board . <p> The Park Board @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ trees in addition to over 50,000 new trees that have been planted in Stanley Park over the last two years . Trees are one of Vancouver 's most important tools for adapting to climate change , but trees themselves are vulnerable to climate change impacts like longer periods of hotter , drier weather . Adopters will care for their trees from June to September when it has n't rained for at least four days . While residents ca n't adopt mature trees , watering all street trees is helpful during dry periods .

@@125428532 <p> Meta 's deal to help revive an Illinois nuclear power plant was one way of signaling that the parent company of Facebook and Instagram is preparing for a future built with artificial intelligence . <p> Meta 's 20-year deal with Constellation Energy follows similar maneuvers from Amazon , Google and Microsoft , but it will take years before nuclear energy can meet the tech industry 's insatiable demand for new sources of electricity . <p> AI uses vast amounts of energy , much of which comes from burning fossil fuels , which causes climate change . The unexpected popularity of generative AI products over the past few years has disrupted many tech companies ' carefully laid plans to supply their technology with energy sources that do n't contribute to climate change . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Even as Meta anticipates more nuclear in the future , its more immediate plans rely on natural gas . Entergy , one of the nation 's largest utility providers , has been fast-tracking plans to build gas-fired power plants in Louisiana to prepare for a massive Meta data center complex . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has touted its ample nuclear power -- which produces about 75% of the nation 's electricity , the highest level in the world -- as a key element in its pitch to be an AI leader . Hosting an AI summit in Paris earlier this year , French President Emmanuel Macron cited President Donald Trump 's " drill baby drill " slogan and offered another : " Here there 's no need to drill , it 's just plug baby plug . " <p> In the U.S. , however , most of the electricity consumed by data centers relies on fossil fuels -- burning natural gas and sometimes coal -- according to an April report from the International Energy Agency . As AI demand rises , the main source of new supply over the coming years is expected to be from gas-fired plants , a cheap and reliable source of power but one that produces planet-warming emissions . <p> Renewable energy sources such as solar and wind account for about 24% of data center power in the U.S. , while nuclear comprises about 15% , according to the IEA . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ including nuclear , could start slowing the expansion of fossil fuel power generation . <p> A report released by the U.S. Department of Energy late last year estimated that the electricity needed for data centers in the U.S. tripled over the past decade and is projected to double or triple again by 2028 when it could consume up to 12% of the nation 's electricity . <p> Why does AI need so much energy ? <p> It takes a lot of computing power to make an AI chatbot and the systems they 're built on , such as Meta 's Llama . It starts with a process called training or pretraining -- the " P " in ChatGPT -- that involves AI systems " learning " from the patterns of huge troves of data . To do that , they need specialized computer chips -- usually graphics processors , or GPUs -- that can run many calculations at a time on a network of devices in communication with each other . <p> Once trained , a generative AI tool still needs electricity to do the work , such as when @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an image . That process is called inferencing . A trained AI model must take in new information and make inferences from what it already knows to produce a response . <p> All of that computing takes a lot of electricity and generates a lot of heat . To keep it cool enough to work properly , data centers need air conditioning . That can require even more electricity , so most data center operators look for other cooling techniques that usually involve pumping in water .

Chr ? tien . <p> In 2018 , the federal government -- the Liberal Justin Trudeau government -- bought the Trans Mountain Pipeline from Kinder Morgan , which was about to give up on it . @@125466666 <h> Does breathing in wildfire smoke mean lung issues for life ? <p> Will unbearable heat and fires become a summertime theme in Canada , and if so , what does this mean for our health ? <p> As a fire rages , carbon dioxide , nitrogen oxide , and fine particulate matter enter the air . These extremely tiny particles are referred to as PM2.5 , essentially measuring 2.5 microns or less in diameter . <p> These particles are problematic because they are small enough to enter our lungs and affect the way we breathe . They can even be small enough to enter our bloodstream and lead to inflammation . <p> This is concerning due to the increased exposure North Americans are facing when it comes to wildfire smoke , and researchers are still revealing what the health effects are when it comes to these events . <p> If we take a look at a few individual fires , the impact on health becomes more apparent . For example , in 2014 , Yellowknife was shrouded in smoke for the entire summer . Dr. Courtney Howard , an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ concrete health conclusions from the event . <p> " We found that we had double the number of emergency department visits over the course of those two and a half months as compared to surrounding years , which is a huge effect , " Dr. Howard explains . " We have a small population , so to show a doubling is big . We had a 50 per cent increase in the dispensing of the breathing medication salbutamol from our pharmacies as people came in with asthma symptoms and needed treatment . We also had an increase in visits to our clinics and our emergency department for pneumonia . " <p> ( Credit : Dr. Courtney Howard/Submitted ) <p> Content continues below <p> Another wildfire that Dr. Howard was able to assess was the historic blaze that took over Fort McMurray , Alta. , in 2016 . She commented on its immense impact on mental health , especially in children , as mass evacuations took over the city . <p> " We all saw those images ; I mean , it was terrifying . And when we examined schoolchildren later @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and depression , as did some of the adults . So we know that those experiences can be really dramatic and scary . " <p> While we still need more concrete evidence on the harm of breathing in wildfire smoke , some studies have started to reveal interesting facts . A study done in B.C. had researchers monitor how long it would take for one 's health to be affected by PM2.5 . The results came in after just one hour of exposure . That same study also drew some conclusions about diabetes and exposure to fine particulate matter . <p> Much of what we know now about health and wildfire smoke can be categorized under immediate effects . What doctors still need to uncover are the long-term effects . As more Canadians experience fire , we wonder : could smoke from one event affect breathing for life ? <p> Currently , Dr. Howard says the best representation in the literature is a study done on monkeys . <p> " They found that those primates had residual lung function problems for their entire lives after an acute episode . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ going to be doing follow-up studies . But for now , we really do n't know what the long-term impacts are of acute exposures to wildfire smoke , especially if they continue to happen more often . " <p> Content continues below <p> And that 's a frightening thought . <p> Are wildfires happening more often ? Will their impact on society and health continue to worsen ? The data shows us that " almost 500,000 Canadians were evacuated due to wildfires between 1980 and 2017 , and half of these evacuations took place in the last decade alone . " <p> It 's clear that our grip on climate change needs to strengthen if we want to properly battle these wildfire events . As of now , the long-term health risks are to be determined ; however , medical professionals know smoky air should be a concern for any population . <p> To learn more about the potential long term impacts of wildfire smoke inhalation , watch the video above .
