@@125547386 <p> The Kiskatinaw River wildfire , located 10 kilometres southwest of Kelly Lake . Discovered on May 28 , 2025 , the wildfire in the Prince George Fire Centre as of June 5 is currently listed as out of control.BC Wildfire Service/X <p> Wildfire season is here and if the last few years are any indication , Canadians will spend the summer sorting through a firestorm of disinformation . <p> People searching for good information in times of crisis are up against a slew of broken systems . Social media algorithms promote misinformation and disinformation and bury official sources . Governments at different levels struggle to coordinate information release as quickly as rumours spread . Not every community has local news and there are fewer reporters and more news deserts . <p> Imperfect information systems and the inherent chaos of a crisis allow well-intentioned but false information to spread , like people making false statements and observations about fire behaviour and what buildings have been destroyed . <p> People 's thirst for information during a crisis creates an information vacuum , and right-wing actors and groups are increasingly filling the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ environmental terrorism , as previously reported by Canada 's National Observer . <p> Some bad information is easier to spot , like baseless claims that wildfires are caused by arson carried out by environmentalists and government actors , or even space lasers . <p> Alberta Premier Danielle Smith fed the flames of disinformation last summer after the town of Jasper was largely destroyed by wildfires . Smith told talk show host Ryan Jespersen the province would bring in arson investigators when he asked about the role climate change played in the 2024 wildfire season . Climate change , driven primarily by burning fossil fuels like coal , oil and gas , is causing higher temperatures and drier conditions , which exacerbate the frequency and severity of wildfires . <p> Maxime Bernier , the far-right People 's Party of Canada leader , went even further during 2023 's record wildfire year , when he said it outright : " I bet a good portion of the wildfires raging across the country were started by green terrorists who want to give their climate change campaign a little boost . " <h> Practical @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ easy task , especially when politicians are participating in the disinformation , but there are some actions we can take to identify or at least remain skeptical about bad information . <p> People should ask themselves , " Does this feel right ? Is this coming from the right place ? Does this seem pretty sensational ? " said Kevin Skrepnek , manager of community and emergency services at the Thompson-Nicola Regional District and BC Wildfire 's former head information officer . <p> " Is this a screenshot of something , or is this an actual link to something ? " <p> Sometimes , old photos are circulated and made to appear recent , so it 's important to think critically about the account or individual that posted an image , what their claims are and whether it 's possible to verify the source of the image . One way to get more information about an image is to do a reverse image search . Sometimes , a simple internet search of the topic at hand combined with the words " fact check " will reveal whether someone has already @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security also recommends checking the spelling of website domains and social media handles , keeping an eye out for small typos that are used to make a site or social media account look like it belongs to an official or trusted organization . <h> When conspiracies impact fire response <p> The most outlandish , viral conspiracies may appear to be confined to the online sphere , but this disinformation can and does have serious impacts on the ground . In 2023 , the BC Wildfire service and police were confronted by a so-called " Convoy of Truth and Freedom , " attempting to gain access to a roadblock while authorities tried to evacuate people and fight the fires in North Shuswap . <p> The agencies responding to fires are " focused on pretty meat and potatoes stuff , " like trying to keep people safe , Skrepnek said -- spending effort addressing " Looney Tunes-level " theories makes it harder to get important information out . <p> Skrepnek emphasized that some people , especially in his rural region , ignore evacuation orders and stay @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ca n't fault them for that . However , he said there is a much smaller -- though growing -- number of people driven by disinformation or distrust of government who resist wildfire evacuation orders on that basis . <p> He said there were issues during the 2021 White Rock Lake fire , when people ignored an evacuation order or sneaked back in because , in their minds , the wildfire service either was n't there or was n't doing enough to defend the remaining properties . <p> " That created a whole issue where now you 've got civilians running around within an evacuation order area trying to fight the fire themselves , getting in the way of the wildfire service in some situations , " Skrepnek said . <p> Getting the right information is key and Skrepnek recommends identifying all the official information channels and bookmarking them so you know where to find updates when a crisis hits . <p> " If your local government or your First Nation or whatever it is , has a subscription-based alerting system , subscribe to that and know that that 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ coming direct from them , " he said . <p> Skrepnek acknowledged this answer wo n't be satisfactory for some people , and government communications wo n't always be perfect , " but that is going to be the best information that you can get . " <p> Relying on information that has been verified by the press or various levels of government is all well and good , but for many remote , rural and Indigenous communities the reality is a lot of information -- good and bad -- circulates on Facebook pages . <h> When getting info from social media is the only option <p> People in remote First Nations communities primarily get their information from social media , said Amy Cardinal Christianson , an Indigenous fire specialist and co-author of two books , one of which is on First Nation wildfire evacuations . <p> Some nations are doing a great job of using Facebook and YouTube livestreams for chiefs to give timely , accurate updates to the community , Christianson said . <p> " But lots of times , misinformation is being shared by us , right @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an answer for a situation , so they see something and immediately post it , " Christianson said . Skrepenk said one citizen-led Facebook group in his region did a good job using a Facebook page to amplify official wildfire information , but said this usually is n't the case , and people often end up sharing unverified information and causing confusion . <p> Many people have good intentions but still contribute to the spread of inaccurate information , Christianson said . <p> " In the past , what we 've seen is people will just post like , ' I heard that so and so 's house burned , ' or ' this burned , ' or ' that burned , ' or ' the fire is here now , ' or ' the fire jumped the river , ' and people immediately just get very upset about that . " <p> Christianson said a good rule of thumb is not to share anything on Facebook or social media if it 's not from an official source or you have n't been able to verify it because things can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , " official " sources might look different for remote communities , she added . <p> " Usually , there 's a contingent of folks in every Indigenous nation that gets evacuated who stay behind , and a lot of that is to do like firefighting or infrastructure protection , to feed dogs or animals that are left behind in the community , " she said . " Those people are often incredibly reliable sources of information for the community . " <p> Critically , these people on the ground are able to dispel rumours and misinformation by confirming what structures have and have n't been affected or answering other questions , according to Christianson 's work studying the 2011 evacuation of Whitefish Lake First Nation in Alberta . <p> In this case , it 's not always as simple as checking whether the government or firefighting agency has corroborated a report or claim because it 's coming from individuals . <p> But Christianson said there are still ways to help assess the reliability of the source , like asking whether they actually have a responsibility or role in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ someone is a trustworthy source , she said . <p> Christianson said most people can weed through the mess of online conspiracies blaming government arson and space lasers , but it does start to create a lack of trust , not just in institutions , but in each other . <p> Times of crisis and big events like wildfires can unite communities , she said . <p> " People forget about differences that they might have and other things , because you 're trying to achieve a common goal together , but the second you start throwing in all this disinformation about arson and who 's starting fires and other things like that , it just really complicates the situation . "

@@125554322 <p> Dr. Gaibrie Stephen is an immigrant , physician and lecturer at the University of Toronto Department of Family and Community Medicine . <p> " Our community is changing . Too many migrants are coming here . " <p> These were n't the words of a Canadian at a town hall -- they came from an older relative in my home village in Kerala , southern India . My relative was referring to the influx of migrant labourers entering Kerala from eastern Indian States . <p> As an Indo-Canadian , the irony of the statement hit me hard . In the same village where young people are queuing for classes in hopes of acing their English language test and leaving for Canada , locals like my uncle were lamenting the arrival of newcomers seeking employment . As a Canadian , I have heard similar unease in my own community . A 2024 survey by the Environics Institute showed that 58 per cent of respondents believe Canada accepts too many immigrants . This is the highest proportion since 1998 . In my small village in India it dawned on me the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ n't the exception -- it 's the rule . <p> Canada , much like Kerala , is grappling with a steep decline in fertility . In 2023 , Canada 's fertility rate hit a record low of 1.26 children per woman ; as of 2023 Kerala 's sits slightly higher at 1.46 . Both fall well below the replacement rate of 2.1 . The result is a shared dilemma : aging populations and growing pressure on health care , pensions , and the labour force . To cope , both places rely increasingly on migration . In Kerala , labourers arrive from Assam , Bihar , and Bangladesh . In Canada , it 's international students , temporary foreign workers , and skilled immigrants . India leads as Canada 's top source country for new permanent residents . <p> Despite the anxiety among locals -- migrants keep both countries running by working in essential sectors like construction , transit , agriculture , and long-term care . And yet , migration often provokes fear , scarcity and in public discourse , the migrants become scapegoats for systemic failures . In Canada @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pace of construction has lagged behind population growth for decades . But instead of zoning laws or speculative markets taking the blame , it 's the newcomers . The same youth my village proudly sends abroad become political flashpoints the moment they land in Canadian cities . <p> There 's a clear pattern of movement . In India , migration is pushed by structural forces like agrarian collapse , unemployment , and climate shocks . Indian workers from vulnerable states are funnelled into more prosperous cities to survive . Zoom out , and the same dynamic unfolds globally : India becomes a source of labour for countries in the Global North like Canada by sending youth , skill , and care to fuel economies . <p> The magnetic pull toward countries like Canada is n't random -- it 's the aftershock of centuries of extraction . Between 1765 and 1938 , colonial powers siphoned an estimated $45 trillion from India , according to economist Utsa Patnaik . That wealth built institutions in the West while leaving former colonies with deep structural deficits . Migration is part of this unfinished story @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ move to find it . <p> Climate change adds a cruel twist . In 2019 , the richest 10 per cent of the global population were responsible for about 48 per cent of global CO2 emissions , while the bottom 50 per cent were responsible for just 12 per cent . Yet it 's countries like Bangladesh , Sudan , and India who are least responsible for the crisis that are hit hardest . Droughts , floods , and rising seas displace millions while the most culpable nations fortify their borders . <p> As Canada 's immigration debate intensifies , it 's important to recognize that reducing the conversation to numbers flattens a far more complex truth . Migration is not the crisis -- it is the response . <p> It is a story shaped by collapsing farms , rising seas , and shrinking futures . @@125554676 <p> I GREW up in Indonesia , the world 's largest island nation , where nature is an incredibly dominant force in daily life . With rainforests , coral reefs , and beaches , Indonesia has some of the most ecologically diverse locations on the planet . <p> But more than just its beautiful nature , Indonesia is also deeply cultural , with traditions and beliefs closely tied to everyone being active stewards of the environment . <p> Raised by Sundanese parents , I learned from them that the way we treat nature is the way nature will treat us . My grandmother always reminded me of this in the guise of a Sundanese saying : Silih asih , silih asah , silih asuh -- to love , to help , and to take care of one another . Caring for nature in her mind was more than about not dropping trash , but it was about putting us on a harmonious footing with the natural world . It is critical in shaping how I see our relationship with the environment today . <p> This wisdom feels more urgent than @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ me to cherish . The Indonesia I know is changing , coastal villages are vanishing , extreme weather is increasing , farmers are experiencing a bitter impact on their crops , Indonesia 's fisheries are at huge risk , and Jakarta , the nation 's capital , is slowly being swallowed up by the sea . For island nations like my own , climate change is n't a future threat ; it 's here and now . <p> Indonesia is not alone in this crisis . As the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change ( UNFCCC ) notes , " Small island nations are extremely susceptible to the impacts of climate change , " and this vulnerability extends across dozens of island countries facing equally grave issues . <h> Headlines Delivered to Your Inbox <h> WORST EFFECTS <p> Although they are the least blameworthy , island countries are facing the worst effects of rising sea levels , severe weather , and crumbling coastlines . In the Caribbean , we are seeing more frequent and powerful hurricanes , coral reef loss , and freshwater shortages , despite contributing a minuscule @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sea level rise of 1.2 millimetres per year over the last three decades . <p> Nevertheless , it is island nations that are taking the lead in addressing the impacts of a changing climate . @@125577159 <p> NEWS RELEASE BROCK UNIVERSITY **25;1227;TOOLONG As any hiker or dog walker can attest , checking for ticks is routine practice after being outdoors at this time of year . But with tick populations on the rise across Ontario , Brock University researchers are looking to spread awareness about the dangers of these pesky bloodsuckers by monitoring local tick populations and testing them for pathogens that can spread diseases to humans and pets . <p> " Tick research is incredibly difficult because of how cryptic ticks can be , " says Biological Sciences PhD student Nick Benton ( MSc ' 24 ) . " Being able to study the abundance and also identify if these ticks are transmitting certain pathogens is important , not only for modelling the exposure risk for the greater community but also seeing trends into how these tick ranges are expanding and potential disease risks in an area . " <p> Benton and a team of Brock researchers are currently collecting and testing ticks found in six areas across Niagara . They 're targeting the Ixodes scapularis ( commonly known as blacklegged ticks or deer ticks @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ causative agent of Lyme disease . Blacklegged ticks have a two-year life cycle that consists of four stages : eggs , larvae , nymphs and adults . <p> Nymphs and adults are currently active , with the team particularly focused on sampling nymphal ticks . These ticks transmit pathogens as well as being exceptionally small , making it much harder to find them on one 's body before they become a health risk . <p> " The adults are the size of sesame seeds , and the nymphs are only the size of poppy seeds , so , imagine trying to find that on your body , " says Benton . <p> Fiona Hunter , a medical and veterinary entomologist at Brock and renowned expert in arthropods such as mosquitoes , says research points to a clear expansion of tick populations across the province . A 2009 study completed by former Brock student Kevin Reeh ( BSc ' 07 , BA ' 10 ) indicated a positive presence of blacklegged ticks in only four of 30 Ontario sites evaluated at the time . That has now increased exponentially . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ virtually anywhere in Niagara and pick up Ixodes scapularis -- that is a major public health concern , " says Hunter , a Professor of Biological Sciences . " We have this deadly tick expanding its range ; it started in southern Ontario , but it 's expanding its range northward . " <p> Evidence points to climate change and warmer temperatures as being one of the main drivers for its population expansion , she says . " They also feed on large ungulates , such as deer , so as deer populations increase , so do Ixodes scapularis populations , " Hunter adds . " They 're also linked to mouse populations , because in the smallest life stages , they 'll feed on mice . In a good year , when you have a lot of acorns , you have a lot of mice and thus a lot of deer ticks . " <p> The good news , the team says , is that ticks do n't begin feeding right away -- so being alert and aware can prevent serious illness . <p> " It 's important to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the longer it feeds on you , the more likely it is to transmit pathogens into your bloodstream , " Benton says . If the tick ca n't easily be brushed off , he recommends removing it with a pair of forceps or tweezers . " The most important thing is to make sure that you 're not damaging the tick by burning , smothering or destroying it , " Benton says . " Get as close to the tick 's head as possible , and gently and slowly pull it straight out , removing as much of the mouthparts as possible and keeping the tick intact . " <p> The team is also on the lookout for the American dog tick ( Dermacentor variabilis ) , groundhog tick ( Ixodes cookei ) , as well as potential other species that can transmit pathogens to humans and animals . While Lyme disease is the most well-known illness spread from tick bites , researchers in Hunter 's lab also test for other tick-borne pathogens : <p> Anaplasma phagocytophilum ( Anaplasmosis ) <p> Babesia microti ( Babesiosis ) <p> Powassan virus ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ spotted fever ) <p> Borrelia bacteria ( Tick-borne relapsing fever ) <p> Although these are much rarer than the pathogen causing Lyme disease , their prevalence in North America is growing , Benton says . <p> " The diseases caused by these pathogens can cause serious symptoms or even death if left untreated , " he adds . " We test for these extra pathogens so the community is aware of their presence and the risks a tick bite from that area can possess . " <p> The research is expected to be completed by mid-summer , with plans to share results with the community . " We want to translate our knowledge and resources into informing the community about potential risks in their environment , " Benton says . " I have a passion for studying insects and for helping people -- so I get to combine my passion for studying arthropods with helping people through medical entomology through this work . "

@@125594172 <p> Mother Nature 's wrath spares no one : man , woman , government , or corporation , the climate crisis is everyone 's business . We all play a role in alleviating or exacerbating the planet 's decline . Yet despite this shared responsibility , why are women in many parts of the world more invested in the climate crisis than men ? <p> In high-income countries , studies consistently show that women are more likely to express alarm or concern about environmental degradation and support policies that combat climate change . Women often lead the way and live more sustainably , from reducing waste to embracing ethical consumption . Meanwhile , men tend to lag behind , showing less concern and fewer efforts to adopt sustainable practices . <p> This disparity is not just a social issue ; it 's a costly setback that hinders our collective ability to address the climate crisis . When half the population is less likely to engage or act on environmental issues , we lose invaluable support for tackling one of the greatest challenges of our time . <h> NUMBERS BEHIND THE @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ registered voters revealed that women are significantly more likely to be climate voters who name climate change or environmental issues as their top political priorities . Sixty-two per cent of climate voters are women , compared to only 37 per cent of men -- an astonishing 25-point gap . <p> Both American men and women think global warming is happening and is caused by human beings , and they believe it at similar levels . Women , however , consistently have higher risk perceptions that global warming will harm them personally , other people in the US , future generations , plants , and animals . They also support certain climate change mitigation policies at higher rates than men . <h> Headlines Delivered to Your Inbox <p> This is n't seen everywhere , though ; the climate gender gap does n't exist in poorer countries and is highly correlated with economic development . Men 's and women 's concerns about global warming are roughly equal in low-income , low per-capita emissions countries and territories . <p> Knowing the statistics is n't enough . To unite people across all economic classes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ need to understand the root causes of the gap and identify actionable steps to close it . <h> WHEN GREEN BECOMES GENDERED <p> One popular theory for the gender gap is that environmentalism is considered feminine , discouraging men from joining the movement because both men and women align " greenness " with femininity . <p> In the US , researchers found men disinclined to engage in any environmentally friendly activity labelled as feminine out of fear of being perceived as being ' soft ' , which included using reusable bags , recycling , and adopting vegetarian or vegan diets . Men may even avoid or actively oppose these green behaviours to protect their gender identity and sense of masculinity . <p> Compared to men , women generally purchase eco-friendly products more frequently , consume less carbon , are more likely to recycle , minimise waste , and save more water and energy . They are also more likely to volunteer for and donate to environmental causes . Harmful stereotypes that equate environmentalism with femininity could discourage some men from embracing these eco-friendly practices . <p> Some research also suggests @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ competitive , women are socialized to be more caring , cooperative , and helpful . This may make women worry more about the environment and , therefore , more willing to adopt eco-friendly behaviours . <p> Women 's higher levels of empathy , altruism , and personal responsibility may make them more interested in environmentalism as a means to protect themselves and others . For example , in a large study in the US , women became more concerned about the impact of climate change and supportive of mitigation policies when asked to consider future generations ; men , meanwhile , experienced no such change . <h> CLIMATE IN THE CLASSROOM <p> Some suggest that women are more environmentally friendly because they 're better educated . It 's often observed that more highly educated people tend to be more environmentally friendly , and women make up the majority of higher education students in 114 countries , compared to only 57 countries with male majorities . In the US , nearly 60 per cent of all undergraduate students are female , while men comprise only 42 per cent . <p> However @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the professions . Furthermore , scientists lack the evidence to identify a causal relationship between higher education and environmentalism in general , and even less to support that the gender gap is a result of their education . <p> Researchers are still divided on a definite cause , and multiple causes may work in tandem . However , integrating climate education across subjects and schools has the potential to shift entrenched behaviours and foster greater awareness and environmentalism regardless of students ' gender identity . <p> One thing is for certain : getting men to care as much as women do is key to saving the planet . Regardless of the gap , at EARTHDAY.ORG , everyone is encouraged to act . You are perfect for the movement as you are , no matter your gender , sexuality , experience level , and more . <p> We may not know for certain how to close the gap . However , all genders can improve their climate education to consume more sustainably , conserve resources , and support the best environmental policies . Take your action to the next level by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tripling renewable energy generation and a Global Plastic Treaty . <p> It 's never too late to get involved . We need a united front to save our planet , so join and spread the movement today . <p> Yasmine Marrero is writing and research intern at EARTHDAY.ORG . @@125615276 <p> Wildfires burning in northern Ontario and the prairies have sparked air quality alerts across the province . <p> Scientists have watched air pollution levels and their potential impacts to human health for more than 20 years . <p> The Air Quality Index was first created to show possible health and environmental impacts to vegetation , visibility and human and animal health . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Initially , it was measured on a scale from 0 to 100 , with specific levels triggering a warning or statement from the ministry . <p> Now called the Air Quality Health Index ( AQHI ) in Canada -- the system is used to warn people who may want to protect their respiratory and visual health . And it 's something used worldwide to monitor air pollution . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> According to Public Health Ontario , the Ontario Ministry of the Environment set up a network of fixed-site air quality monitoring stations in municipalities around the province around 2003 . <p> They were looking for different substances in the air . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <h> Air pollutants <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the government is testing for air quality . <h> Fine particulate matter <p> Fine particulate matter is small particles of solids and aerosols mixed together , which can include metallic compounds , elemental carbon , organic compounds , and compounds from the Earth . Scientifically known as PM2.5 , they are 2.5 microns or less in diameter and can be inhaled and absorbed by the lungs . <p> Sources include burning gasoline , oil , diesel fuel or wood . <p> " Those are things from forest fire or wildfire smoke , they are very fine particles in the atmosphere that can be irritants to the general public , especially those with pre-existing health conditions , " said Steven Flisfeder , a warning preparedness meteorologist with Environment and Climate Change Canada . <p> That 's what we 're seeing in higher volumes this week , as uncontrolled wildfires burn in the prairies and northern Ontario . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <h> Ground-level ozone <p> The second substance is ozone , known as O3 , and we typically see higher levels in the springtime , before tree leaves come out . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . We hear about ozone in the upper atmosphere , which is helpful to protect from solar radiation , " Flisfeder said . " Once it reaches the surface level , it can cause adverse health effects . " <h> Nitrous dioxide <p> The AQHI also looks for nitrous dioxide , or NO2 , which is essentially car exhaust . <p> " We 've been seeing them stay below our threshold that would trigger an air quality statement , " Flisfeder said . " We tend to see a spike in nitrous dioxide during the rush hour when more people are out on the roads , but if the atmosphere is in a state where those ( fumes ) are able to rise and dissipate , they wo n't get to a concentration that would warrant an air quality statement . " <h> Health impacts <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Health Canada estimates that above-background air pollution , including air pollution from human sources in North America , contributes to 15,300 premature deaths per year in Canada . <p> In fact , air pollution is the fifth leading mortality risk @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Disease project . <p> Back in 2016 , Health Canada said the total economic cost of all health impacts -- attributable to air pollution for the year -- was estimated at $120 billion . <p> Exposure to any of these air pollutants can cause coughing and sore or scratchy throat , make it more difficult to take a deep breath . It may cause wheezing or can be painful when taking a deep breath . It can irritate your eyes , nose and throat . <p> Levels one to three are within normal range -- no caution is needed . They are colour-coded with blue colours . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Levels four to six mean there 's a moderate risk . For those with asthma or chronic health issues , they may notice a change with breathing when outdoors . They are colour-coded in yellow and orange , to show there 's a caution . <p> " You do n't really need to modify your daily activities , but if you start experience systems , such as coughing or sore throat , then take preventive action , " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and stop any strenuous outdoor activity , he added . <p> Levels seven to 10 are high risk , and are marked with shades of red . <p> " That 's where everybody should start to consider reducing or rescheduling their outdoor activities . It 's not just about waiting to see if you have these outdoor irritations , " he said . <p> The final , 10-plus level is considered very high risk , a dark red or maroon colour is used for this level , and everyone may experience side effects from the poor air quality . <p> Each individual pollutant has a safe range , and if any one is elevated , Environment Canada meteorologists can issue an air quality alert . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> " Right now we have forest fire smoke that is reaching the surface in high concentrations , " Flisfeder said . " Fine particulate matter -- what we refer to as PM2.5 -- when those concentrations reach at least 60 microns , which is micrograms per metre cubed , it automatically forces our hand to issue an air quality @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ formula that checks the cumulative effects of all three pollutants , which can also trigger an alert . <h> Atmospheric levels <p> For humans to be impacted by the air pollution , it has to be within breathing level . <p> Meteorologists use the term surface level when monitoring AQHI . <p> " In meteorology , we refer to surface level as the lowest levels of the atmosphere . So anywhere from the ground we walk on or the waters , up to a few hundred meters that can be low enough that it affects air quality . " <p> Already this year , wildfire smoke has drifted southward , but it 's been so high up in the atmosphere that it has n't impacted the air we breathe , and no alerts were issued . <p> " When it 's higher up in the atmosphere , you can still see the effects , but it does n't have any health affects for most people . You can see the hazy skies at sunset and sunrise . You see a red sun instead of a typical orange or yellow sun @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ atmosphere but it 's not making its way low enough to impact general health . " <h> Winds of change <p> It is interesting to see how far the winds carry forest fire smoke , which can impact us in Ontario from several provinces away . <p> " All that smoke becomes concentrated in the atmosphere at varying levels , so it 's not all at surface level , " Flisfeder said . " As the winds push it east or west or north or south -- wherever it happens to go -- those concentrations change at different places . It can travel across the country . It can go all the way across the world as well . " <p> And because some of that smoke is already in the atmosphere , if all of the forest fires were put out tomorrow , we could still see residual effects for a few days . <p> " I would n't be an expert on that , there are dissipation models run on a regular basis . Typically speaking , if the fires were put out tomorrow , the concentrations already @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cycle , " Flisfeder said . " It can last in the atmosphere . " <p> The likelihood you might smell smoke from wildfires elsewhere all depends on the concentration of particles , Flisfeder said . <p> " The higher the concentration , that would relate to a higher AQHI number . It is primarily used to treat cancer but is expanding into incurable diseases such as autoimmune disease and heart fibrosis . <p> " Cell therapies have enormous potential to treat patients with a disease or injury that requires replacement or repair , " explained Dr. April Pyle @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ molecular genetics at the University of California , Los Angeles ' ( UCLA 's ) Broad Stem Cell Research Center . " They can be used to directly deliver new cells to patients in need of cells in a particular tissue or organ system . " <p> " These cells could be isolated from a matched donor ( allogeneic ) , or isolated from a patient , then processed in the lab and reinfused to the same patient ( autologous ) , " added Dr. Ahmed Gad , a postdoctoral associate in pediatric hematology , oncology and cell and gene therapy at Baylor College of Medicine . <p> This broad definition means blood transfusions and bone marrow transplants are considered types of cell therapy , but more recently , the term is used to refer to the transfer of a particular cell population , including stem cells and immune cells . <p> Cell-based therapies , such as stem cell-based therapies and CAR T-cell therapies , are transforming healthcare , but what does the future hold for them and how can we overcome the barriers to their expansion ? <h> Immune @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ particular immune cell population and use it for therapeutic intervention . The first to receive US Food and Drug Administration ( FDA ) approval was sipuleucel-T , a dendritic cell ( DC ) therapy for men with advanced prostate cancer that had not responded to hormone therapy . <p> Gad describes sipuleucel-T as " kind of a hack to the system " with DCs acting as " professional antigen-presenting cells " that detect foreign antigens originating from pathogens , mutated proteins or foreign tissues . DCs travel to an injured site , ingest proteins , digest them into small peptides ( epitopes ) and present them on their surface with human leukocytic antigen ( HLA ) , before moving to the lymph nodes where T cells and B cells reside . <p> Human leukocytic antigen ( HLA ) <p> HLA molecules are cell surface proteins whose primary function is to present endogenous and exogenous antigens to T cells for recognition . In other words , they help the body 's immune system identify foreign cells . <p> During treatment , a patient 's DCs are isolated and incubated in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reinfused into the patient to activate T cells -- what Gad calls " professional assassins " -- that seek out and destroy cancerous cells displaying HLA and foreign antigens specific to the prostate cancer proteins . <p> The FDA has since approved multiple T-cell therapy products , including those with transgenic T-cell receptors ( tgTCRs ) or chimeric antigen receptors ( CARs ) . <h> CAR T-cell therapy and cancer <p> Gad 's lab focuses on CAR T-cell therapy ( Figure 1 ) , " a form of engineered T-cell therapy that brings the best of two worlds together " . Used mainly in oncology , patient-derived T cells are " engineered to express a synthetic surface receptor that has the antigen binding domain of an antibody fused to the TCR signaling machinery ; this fusion is what gives it the name ' chimeric ' , " he explained . <p> Figure 1 : In CAR T-cell therapy , T cells are isolated from the blood and genetically modified to express cancer-targeting CARs . Engineered cells are then expanded and administered back to the patient . Credit : Technology Networks @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ efficiency.View Infographic <p> Advertisement <p> Antibodies have " the superb ability to identify proteins in their intact form with no need for digestion and presentation on HLA , " Gad continued . When a CAR 's antibody-derived antigen-binding domain identifies a tumor cell 's surface antigen , it forms an immune synapse -- an interaction site between the CAR T cell and the tumor cell . This triggers downstream signaling , recruiting co-activatory , co-inhibitory and adhesion molecules to the immune synapse . These interactions lead CAR T cells to recruit lethal mechanisms to the immune synapse to kill the cancer cell . <p> Gad said CAR T-cell therapy is " compatible with any patient 's cancer and can be easily engineered against any tumor-associated surface protein . " His lab pioneers the development of HER2 CAR T-cell therapy for treating brain and bone/sarcoma cancers . <p> To better understand the determinants of CAR T-cell success on the microscopic level , Gad 's research focuses on the CAR immune synapse ( CARIS ) , the " battlefront between a CAR T cell and a cancer cell " , and the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ into the tactics used by both the CAR T cells and tumor cells during their fight and can drive the engineering of CAR T cells with better therapeutic capacities . In their recent research paper , Gad and colleagues found that the two most common designs of CAR T cell -- CD28 signaling and 41BB signaling CAR T cells -- use two different killing strategies . <p> " CD28 CAR T cells are serial killers , " Gad explained . " They have the ability to kill a cancer cell fast and move to kill others . " They succeed because they have brief synapse interactions , " in which they can converge toxic granules ' grenades ' toward the synapse and release them onto the tumor cell . These grenades make pores in the cell membrane of the tumor cell through which toxic proteins get in to kill it . " <p> The second design , 41BB CAR T cells , Gad describes as ' cooperative killers ' : " When they see the tumor , they expand into more CAR T cells . Multiple CAR T cells then @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more protracted interaction that rely on a more chronic killing machinery , which is the chronic interaction between Fas ligands on CAR-T with Fas receptors on the surface of tumor cells . " <p> On the molecular level , Gad found that CAR T cells use special membrane microdomains called lipid rafts to recruit functional receptors to the CARIS . These rigid islands that float on the surface of the fluid cell membrane provide structural and functional support at the immune synapse . <p> Gad 's research found that the dynamics of CAR interaction with lipid rafts influence the cancer-killing behavior of CAR T cells . " For example , the brief cellular interactions that CD28 CAR T cells have with cancer cells are a reflection of the brief molecular interactions between CD28 CAR molecules and CAR T cell membrane lipid rafts , " Gad explained . <p> " In the same sense , 41BB CAR T-cell protracted CARIS correlates with protracted interactions between 41BB CAR molecules and CAR T cell membrane lipid rafts . " <p> Pyle and her @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ human skeletal muscle . They identified various cell types , but focused on muscle progenitor cells , which form muscles before birth , and muscle stem cells , which aid muscle formation after birth and regeneration from injury throughout life . <p> The researchers charted how the cells ' gene networks changed as cells mature , locating the precise networks present in muscle progenitor and stem cells across development . Most targeted biological therapies and CAR T-cell therapies @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ can laser-target tumor cells with much less side effects compared to chemo- and radiotherapy , " Gad said . @@125656297 <p> THUNDER BAY -- There are no air quality monitoring stations between Thunder Bay and Winnipeg , but a number of commercially-available sensors are helping to fill in the picture on air quality in the region . <p> Multiple levels of government and other organizations have partnered up to promote the installation of the relatively inexpensive air quality sensors nation-wide , helping to make data and forecasting more detailed . <p> The initiative is a partnership between Environment and Climate Change Canada , Health Canada , provincial environment ministries and other local authorities . Keith Jones , the head of the air quality science unit at the Meteorological Service of Canada , said a recently-completed five-year pilot project saw the installation of about 450 additional sensors across Canada that specifically measure fine particulate matter -- the name for a range of tiny particles found in many types of air pollution , including forest fire smoke . <p> It is dangerous to human health because it travels deep into the lungs , causing a host of health problems . <p> " These sensors can be purchased by anybody -- individuals or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " A lot of these sensors are just out there , purchased by other individuals , and the data is available to be viewed as well . " <p> An interactive map was developed in partnership with the University of Northern British Columbia , Jones said , where people can check the readings of each individual sensor that is registered with the program . <p> This network is intended to help expand the amount of information available about fine particulate matter across the country , leading to more detailed data collection and forecasting used to inform the issuing of air quality alerts , Jones said . <p> These sensors compliment the network of larger air quality health index ( AQHI ) observation stations in place . People intuitively understand what urgency is , but what is human agency , a complex concept explored in philosophy , psychology , and other social sciences ? Understanding fully that our agency is key to managing climate change can help mobilize stronger and more effective climate action . <p> Human agency can operate at personal , group , organizational , community , country , and species levels . It combines thinking and acting to achieve desired results -- here , to take more meaningful and high-impact climate actions . <p> Meaningful impact and constant progress require knowing what to do and then doing it . We already know what we need to do and how to do it : reduce fossil fuel use as much and as soon as possible and replace it with renewable energy sources to slow and eventually stop global heating . You only need to initiate a few that suit you best based on experience , knowledge , or interests . @@125727934 <p> Althia Raj is a national politics columnist for the Star . Follow her on Twitter : @althiaraj <p> They say a picture is worth a thousand words . And so on Friday , when Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a new omnibus bill that gives cabinet the right to circumvent environmental laws in the name of getting big resource projects built , perhaps it was noteworthy that Environment and Climate Minister Julie Dabrusin was not one of the five cabinet ministers serving as the prime minister 's backdrop . <p> The bill is actually two pieces of legislation which have nothing to do with one another . The first part , the Free Trade and Labour Mobility in Canada Act , has widespread support and could easily pass the House of Commons . The second part , the Building Canada Act , is the type of legislation that Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper might have been too timid to bring forward , fearing a public backlash . It hands over sweeping decision-making powers to one cabinet minister in untransparent ways , gives cabinet the ability to delete environmental laws @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be looked at with a fine-tooth comb . Despite the vehement opposition of the Bloc Qu ? b ? cois , the NDP , and the Green Party , it may still sail through the Commons with the support of the Conservatives . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> The Building Canada Act would allow cabinet , for a period of five years , to give the green light to projects that it believes are in the national interest , based on a loose set of factors that could shift depending on the whim of this -- or any future -- government . Those factors could include : whether a project strengthens Canada 's autonomy , resilience and security ; whether it provides economic or other benefits to the country ; whether it has a high likelihood of successful execution ; whether it advances the interest of Indigenous Peoples ( as defined by the government ) ; and whether it contributes to clean growth and meeting Canada 's objectives with respect to climate change ( though it does n't say what specific objectives ) . <p> Only after the prime minister @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , does the government start to consider what conditions to place upon the project . " It would be kind of like giving somebody a driver 's license and then asking them to take the road test . It just does n't make sense , " said Anna Johnston , a staff lawyer with West Coast Environmental Law and a member of the environment minister 's advisory council on impact assessment . <p> Following a review process , triggered by , for example , the Canadian Navigable Waters Act , the Species at Risk Act , the Migratory Birds Convention Act , the Fisheries Act , the Impact Assessment Act , etc. , the ministers responsible would hand over recommendations for conditions to place upon a project to a designated minister -- in this case Intergovernmental Affairs Minister Dominic LeBlanc . The law is silent on the timeline , though the government 's stated goal is two years . The law is also silent on whether the recommendations flowing from the reviews would be made public . In fact , the law currently allows LeBlanc to pick and choose which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ under no legal obligation to impose any of the conditions that were recommended to him . <p> Imagine the scale of the lobbying effort that will be deployed , or the lawsuits that will flow once project proponents realize they were n't subject to the same rules and considerations that their competitors were . <p> This bill also allows cabinet to ignore laws it does n't want to abide by . For example , if the government is worried about the outcome of a review triggered by the Canadian Environmental Protection Act , it could delete that act from consideration . If the minority Liberal government is defeated next year the law would allow the next prime minister , say current Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre , to delete all 13 laws and seven regulations used to evaluate and consider such projects . <p> What 's more there is no mechanism through which public consultations can result in a project 's green light turning into a red light . No matter how hard the public screams or what facts emerge from the review , the only consideration in the law right @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ remains in the national interest . @@125733464 <p> Smoke from wildfires has already led Environment Canada to issue air quality warnings for much of Ontario . In Toronto , smoke led to the city briefly having the worst air quality in the world . <p> Anyone who has experienced wildfire smoke knows how it can leave you with a scratchy throat , stinging eyes and impact your lungs . However , smoke can also affect your brain . Tiny airborne pollutants found in smoke have been linked to increased risk of stroke , dementia and flare-ups in neurological diseases like multiple sclerosis ( MS ) . <p> These effects can disproportionately impact older adults , people with disabilities , Indigenous Peoples and those living in low-income communities . This is n't just about climate . It 's about equity , and health systems need to catch up . <p> Canada 's 2023 wildfire season was the worst on record , and as climate change worsens wildfires , it may be a sign of what 's to come . <h> A direct path to the brain <p> Alongside harmful gases and heavy metals , wildfire smoke contains fine @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ particles can travel deep into your lungs , slip into your bloodstream and even reach your brain . Some even bypass the lungs entirely , entering the brain directly through the nose . <p> Content continues below <p> After entering the brain , these toxins can cause inflammation and stress , damage nerve cells and even accelerate cognitive decline . Studies have linked exposure to air pollution to an increased risk of stroke and dementia . Even short-term spikes in smoke exposure , like those during wildfires , lead to a surge in emergency visits for strokes , especially among people over 65 . <p> A 2022 experiment had thousands of adults participate in an online attention task under smoky conditions . It found that just a three-hour spike in fine particulate matter , typical of a heavy smoke episode , led to measurably worse attention scores . This fits other evidence that breathing smoke makes people mentally foggy , forgetful or fatigued . <p> For people already living with neurological conditions like MS or Parkinson 's disease , the stakes are even higher . Exposure to fine particulate pollution @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , particularly in young patients . Other research points to worsening symptoms of epilepsy and cognitive decline under extreme heat and polluted air conditions . <p> Despite these mounting risks , neurological health considerations have been largely absent from wildfire preparedness initiatives and public health responses . That needs to change . <p> Content continues below <p> If you want to stay informed about local smoke exposure , tools like AQmap can help you track PM2.5 levels in real time across Canada . <p> Each of these groups faces unique and compounding challenges during smoke events . For example , older adults are more vulnerable to the cardiovascular and neurological effects of smoke . They also face greater barriers to accessing filtered environments . <p> People with disabilities or chronic illnesses , including those with neurological conditions , often ca n't relocate during smoke events and may rely on power-dependent medical devices that can fail during climate emergencies . <p> Low-income families are more likely to live in housing without proper air filtration or cooling . These same communities often face higher baseline rates of neurological disease . <p> Children @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of wildfires . Because their brains are still developing and they breathe more air per body weight than adults , children are especially vulnerable to harmful pollutants . <p> These populations are n't just more exposed , they also have fewer resources to respond . <h> WATCH BELOW : Tips to help protect yourself from wildfire smoke <h> Rethinking Canada 's health systems <p> Recognizing these inequities , we are developing a climate-health equity framework for Canada , with a specific focus on neurological health . Our interdisciplinary team is asking : how can we build health systems that protect vulnerable brains during climate emergencies ? <p> Public awareness must expand beyond respiratory health . Neurological effects of smoke should be included in public health messaging , especially for high-risk groups . <p> Health systems must be climate-ready , with clean air shelters , evacuation protocols and services tailored to meet the needs of neurological patients . <p> Communities need support , from funding for air filtration to co-ordinated outreach during smoke events . Indigenous-led fire stewardship and community health initiatives should be part of national planning . Supporting Indigenous-led @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Indigenous sovereignty and traditional ecological knowledge . <p> Clinicians must be empowered to address climate-related health risks . Training in environmental health , including its impact on the brain , is increasingly essential . <p> Wildfire season is back , and with it , an urgent need to protect more than just our lungs . The science is clear : breathing smoky air affects our minds , especially for those already facing health and social vulnerabilities . <p> Climate change is a brain health issue . Building a healthier , more equitable future requires us to treat it that way , starting now .

What once was notable is becoming a habit , a toxic , sinister pattern . @@125737360 <p> The bill , tabled Friday , defines a " major project " as one that contributes to national prosperity , strengthens economic resiliency , advances the interests of Indigenous people and meets climate change objectives . If a project meets these criteria , it would benefit from streamlined approval and , presumably , a whack of federal cash . <p> Let 's hope , however , that this is n't all about pipelines , power plants and other bricks-and-mortar infrastructure projects . Because there 's something missing in the selection criteria : Values . <p> The most impactful nation-building projects are not things , but ideas -- programs that focus on bettering the health of people , both physically and financially . <p> Case in point : Medicare . <p> The underlying philosophy of Canadian medicare is that no one should be denied essential care because of an inability to pay . <p> It results in big costs savings for individuals . In the U.S. , suffocating medical bills are the top cause of personal bankruptcy ; in Canada , that is almost unheard of . <p> Medicare is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ premiums . It 's also an economic stimulus and stabilizer . Having a massive , publicly funded health infrastructure , with 2.1 million employees , helps recession-proof Canada , as was demonstrated during both the 2008-09 financial market crisis , and the height of the COVID-19 pandemic . <p> Canada also has the Non-Insured Health Benefits ( NIHB ) program , a publicly funded type of health insurance specifically for Indigenous peoples that is more expansive than medicare . <p> But provincial and territorial medicare programs , and the NIHB , are outdated and struggling to meet the needs of a 21st-century population . Reforming medicare could be profoundly impactful on national scale . <p> What better nation-building project could there be than bolstering programs that are not only uniquely Canadian but distinguish us clearly from Americans ? ( Not to mention that a smart investment in medicare would meet all the criteria for a " nation-building " project worthy of fast-tracking . ) <p> The other component of " nation building , " especially in these patriotic times , should be building pride , not just physical stuff . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . As Mr. Trump 's America slashes its contributions to global health initiatives in an orgy of self-centredness , there is tremendous opportunity for Canada to step up . <p> " If the U.S. no longer wants to lead , Canada will , " Prime Minister Carney said back in April . He was talking about the importance of international co-operation on trade , but that philosophy could and should apply to other areas of global policy . <p> There is currently a campaign to end the scourge of HIV-AIDS by 2030 . In the wake of COVID-19 , which sapped all public health resources for years , that goal was already in peril , and now U.S. cuts could bury it . <p> Imagine if Canada made this its cause . <p> HIV-AIDS has infected an estimated 88.4 million people , 39.9 million of whom are still alive . Thirty million of those survivors are currently taking antiretroviral drugs that suppress the virus . <p> If we could get the other 10 million on treatment , further infections would virtually disappear . <p> Treatment as prevention is a Canadian @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has already saved millions of lives . <p> Ironically though , within Canada , only B.C. has embraced it , while other provinces have dithered . The greatest beneficiaries of a treatment-as-prevention strategy could be Indigenous communities , where HIV rates are soaring , especially in Manitoba and Saskatchewan . <p> Imagine a Canada without HIV , or AIDS . A world without either . <p> That could be a bold Canadian goal , one worthy of our ambitions . Soft power suits us better than hard power . <p> All this may seem fanciful , a far cry from our traditional view of nation-building projects . <p> But let 's not forget we have a Prime Minister who has spoken and written eloquently on the importance of socially motivated investing , on the importance of putting purpose before profit . <p> In his 2021 book , Value(s) : Building A Better World For All , Mr. Carney reflects thoughtfully on the corrosive impact of inequality and unhealthiness , and how more equal societies are more resilient . <p> He also writes about seven key values that are essential for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , resilience , sustainability , dynamism , and humility , all laced with compassion . <p> The way to embrace those values is to invest in programs that make people healthier and more equal , like medicare , and ending AIDS . <p> Economically , and otherwise , we should take that over a pipeline any day .

@@125738038 <h> Using AI to protect caribou migration in a changing Arctic <h> Share this article <p> A machine learning tool is offering new hope for one of Canada 's most vulnerable caribou migrations . <p> Researchers are turning to artificial intelligence to predict when and where the Dolphin and Union caribou will cross the sea ice between Victoria Island and the mainland of Nunavut -- a migration that takes place each spring and fall but has become more dangerous as climate change thins the ice and shipping traffic climbs . <p> Caribou can drown if they try to cross ice that is unstable , and the risk increases when icebreakers and other vessels move through the area -- and the ships are arriving in greater numbers than ever before . The tool called IceNet can help protect caribou by warning when migration conditions may be dangerous . <p> " Climate change is causing Arctic sea ice to recede and become less stable -- which also means the region is becoming more accessible for ships , " said Ellen Bowler , a machine learning research scientist at the British Antarctic Survey @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Alan Turing Institute , the World Wildlife Fund and Nunavut government . " This combination of threats could have fatal consequences for iconic animals like caribou . " <h> Saving a vanishing herd <p> The Dolphin and Union caribou herd once numbered around 100,000 but dropped sharply in the early 1900s . The population grew again later in the century , but that recovery did not last . By 1997 , there were about 34,000 caribou , and by 2020 , only around 3,800 remained . When numbers dropped very low in the past , the migration even stopped for a time . <p> Elders and local hunters have reported even sharper declines , more sick and skinny animals , and fewer calves surviving . In 2017 , the herd was officially listed as endangered , with experts warning of " imminent extinction " if these threats continue . <p> " Instead of just forecasting sea ice concentration , we can actually start to forecast when they 're most likely to migrate in a given year , " Ellen Bowler , a machine learning research scientist at the British Antarctic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ collected by government agencies , Inuit hunters and community researchers , the new AI system can predict the start of caribou migration up to three weeks in advance -- giving vessel operators time to adjust their routes or pause shipping during this critical migration period . <p> " Instead of just forecasting sea ice concentration , we can actually start to forecast when they 're most likely to migrate in a given year , " Bowler said . <p> A small cabin stands isolated on a frozen lake on the south coast of the Victoria Islands , surrounded by snow-covered tundra and ice ridges . Photo by Terry Milton / Government of Nunavut . <p> Brandon Laforest , lead specialist for Arctic conservation at WWF Canada , works directly with Inuit communities on conservation priorities in Nunavut . He said that the technology offers a promising solution to a well-documented problem . <p> Inuit hunters and elders have seen caribou hesitate at the ice edge , fall through or abandon their usual crossing spots . Bleaching occurs when stressed corals expel the algae living within them , causing the corals to lose their characteristic colours and putting them at greater risk of death . Coral reefs ' ecosystems sustain various marine species , so the loss of reefs have broader impacts . <p> Corals living in waters with frequent temperature swings are better at surviving extreme heat than are corals in waters with more stable temperatures , the researchers found . This suggests that their resilience depends not only on their genes , but on their environment . The stability of the algae and bacteria living inside the coral was also found to play a role . These microbial allies include symbiotic algae , which provide energy , and bacteria , which help regulate stress and disease . <p> " Understanding what makes some corals more resilient to increasing temperatures helps us figure out how reefs might survive climate change and where to focus conservation efforts , " said Victoria Glynn , lead author of the study , who conducted the work as a PhD @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The team studied coral reefs in two regions of Panama 's Tropical Eastern Pacific , each with very different ocean conditions . In the Gulf of Panama , strong seasonal upwelling -- a process that causes cold water to rise toward the surface -- brings rapid fluctuations in temperature and water chemistry . In the Gulf of Chiriqu ? , conditions are much more stable . <p> To test how corals from each region respond to extreme heat , the researchers collected samples and used a specialized lab system called the Coral Bleaching Automated Stress System ( CBASS ) , which mimics marine heatwaves , allowing observation of how corals respond to sudden stress . <p> They also analyzed the coral 's genetic background and their microbiomes -- algal and bacterial communities -- of each coral and tracked physiological changes like antioxidant capacity and protein content . <h> More heat tolerance in corals from unstable waters <p> Despite sharing much of the same DNA , corals from the Gulf of Panama were more heat-tolerant than those from the Gulf of Chiriqu ? . <p> In lab tests , Gulf @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ damage more effectively than did their counterparts from the more stable Chiriqu ? . However , the team also found that bacterial microbiomes from both locations corals became more unstable and variable under heat stress , a sign of bleaching vulnerability . <p> One of the study 's most surprising findings challenges conventional wisdom about coral-algae relationships . While many stressed corals in other regions switch to Durusdinium algae -- associated with higher heat tolerance some corals often retained Cladocopium at high temperatures , which provides more energy but less heat protection . <p> " This suggests there 's a trade-off between energy supply and heat resistance , " said Barrett . <h> Implications for reef survival <p> The findings support the idea that corals regularly exposed to variable conditions may be " pre-adapted " to future climate extremes . This weak rotation is normally not a danger near the ground . However , there is a chance that this rotation could intensify and become a weak landspout tornado . If conditions become more favourable for the development of landspout tornadoes , watches and warnings will be issued by Environment Canada . Landspout tornadoes do not usually cause significant damage but can still be dangerous . They can be strong enough to topple trees , damage roofs or toss debris short distances . Treat any funnel cloud sighting seriously . Should a funnel cloud develop nearby , prepare to take shelter . These funnel clouds usually appear with little or no warning .

Contact him at Bullockm@Nexicom.net or 705-741-6283 . <p> Those who are deeply concerned about climate change tend to think of themselves as a minority . The slow and halting progress we have made toward addressing climate change , and particularly the reluctance of governments to take effective action , might seem to suggest they are correct . <p> The fact is , however , those who care deeply about climate change and want to see more government action to address it are not a minority at all , but the majority . Most people in countries around the world , including Canada , are concerned about the climate , and want to see more government action . <p> A number of recent studies have shown the vast majority of people worldwide are aware of the threat climate change poses to our future and want their governments to do more in response . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ which surveyed 130,000 people across 125 countries , found that globally , 89 per cent of people favoured greater action by government . It also found 69 per cent of people would be willing to contribute one per cent of their income to help reduce climate change . <p> The study also found people consistently underestimate how concerned their fellow citizens are about climate , and the degree to which they support climate action . For example , people estimated that just 43 per cent of their fellow citizens would be willing to give one per cent of their income to fight climate change -- 26 per cent lower than the actual number . <p> Another study , Peoples ' Climate Vote 2024 , by the United Nations Development Programme and the University of Oxford , found that 80 per cent of people globally want stronger climate action from their own government -- and 72 per cent want their country to quickly replace coal , oil and gas as energy sources with renewable energy , such as electricity generated from the wind and the sun . <h> Greater concern among @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ concern about climate , and the desire for more climate action by government , were greater in poorer and middle-income countries than in wealthier ones . The Global Climate Change survey concluded richer countries were more likely to possess the resources to adapt to a changing climate , and that their high incomes were dependent on their use of fossil fuels . <p> The Global Climate Change Survey also concluded that people in warmer countries , which were more likely to be already experiencing the adverse effects of climate change , were , on average , more willing to give up income to combat climate change , and more desirous of greater climate action by government . <h> Canadian opinion favours action <p> Canada is a rich , industrialized , northern country , and this is reflected in survey results . People 's Climate Vote 2024 found that 66 per cent of Canadians want more climate action from government , and that 65 per cent favoured a quick transition from coal , oil and gas to renewable energy . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> There are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ one hand , in comparison to the global average , a smaller proportion of Canadians want to see stronger climate action from government and a rapid energy transition . On the other hand , a solid majority of Canadians do want these things , and this is , or should be , a significant political fact . <p> The 2025 federal election illustrates the point . There is no doubt the campaign saw climate change , as a political issue , pulled back from centre stage and bundled off to somewhere in the wings . Pierre Poilievre was hoping for a " carbon tax election " in which he could make effective use of his " axe the tax " slogan . This did not materialize , in part because Mark Carney did away with consumer carbon pricing as one of his first acts as prime minister , thereby ensuring the election would be fought on other issues . <p> In the run-up to the election , just four per cent of eligible voters reported climate change was the most important issue . <p> Where , then , is the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ action ? <p> Climate change , as a political issue , was partially submerged , like other issues , by the overwhelming importance attached to the defence of national sovereignty . Yet poll results showed Canadians still cared about climate change . <p> An Angus Reid poll found climate change ranked sixth on voters ' list of priorities -- not insignificant -- and it was on the issue of climate change that the ultimately victorious Liberals enjoyed their greatest lead -- 83 per cent over their Conservative opponents . <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW <p> Carney 's personal commitment to climate change action is strong , and a well-known element of his resum ? . After he was governor of the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England , he was both the United Nations special envoy on climate action and finance , and the United Kingdom 's finance adviser at COP26 . <p> Carney 's book , " Value(s) " , sets out how reforms to international financial institutions could redirect investment dollars away from fossil fuel projects and toward the development of renewable energy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ number of actions on the climate front : improvements to the Output Based Pricing System for pricing industrial carbon ; a carbon border adjustment mechanism ( an import tariff to protect Canadian industry from foreign competitors which are allowed to emit higher levels of CO2 ) ; enhanced methane regulations for oil and gas producers ; support for clean energy projects ; the expansion of the EV charging network ; and the phase out of fossil fuel use in government buildings . <p> In the voting , 57.5 per cent of ballots cast nationally were for parties with strong climate change platforms . Of the two leading parties , the Liberals and the Conservatives , it was the victorious Liberals who unambiguously favoured vigorous climate action . The election gave Carney and his government a strong mandate to act on climate change . <h> Strengthening the Canadian economy <p> The manner in which Canada deals with the challenges it now confronts will set our direction for many years . There are opportunists who would like nothing better than to use our situation as a pretext for pursuing economic growth at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to climate change . This was certainly the case with the 38 CEOs of Canadian oil and gas companies who , on the day after the election , sent Carney their wish list , which included the elimination of the emissions cap on oil and gas production and the end of industrial carbon pricing . <p> Carney should reject these sorts of demands , for a number of reasons . In the absence of a concerted global effort to stop climate change , its many costs , which we are already paying , will grow at an accelerating rate . Addressing climate change in a timely and effective manner will directly benefit the Canadian economy ; as Carney himself has argued , there is a huge economic opportunity in the transition away from fossil fuels and toward renewable energy . <p> There is also this : a solid majority of Canadians , just like a majority of people around the globe , want their government to do more , not less , to ensure that we bequeath to our children a planet upon which they and their children can flourish @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ week on behalf of Drew Monkman . C , and in these conditions , it can take around 10 days to go from an egg to an adult . <p> While these factors turn any area into a mosquito hotspot , there are some parts of Canada that see more activity than others . <h> Canada 's mosquito hotspots <p> We would be remiss if we failed to mention Komarno , Manitoba , located an hour north of Winnipeg . Mosquitos are so prevalent here the community established a giant mosquito monument , commemorating their presence each summer , as well as the rural municipality 's name , which is a Ukrainian word for " lots of mosquitoes . " <p> Northern Manitoba and the boreal forest . Further north , Manitoba 's boreal forest has an abundance of vegetation and wetlands , two things mosquitoes love . This region is considered the " mosquito capital " of the territory . Mosquito season used to be brief here , historically lasting between 4 and 6 weeks . Thanks to climate change , experts say the season is getting longer : Mosquitoes are arriving earlier and sticking around longer . <p> Algonquin Provincial Park , Ontario . Dense forests and more than 1,500 lakes means this park experiences a lot of mosquito activity . especially in cooler , shaded areas . Thankfully , you can check the mosquito forecast before heading out on the trail . <p> Northern British Columbia and Yukon . Climate change is extending mosquito season in these regions . There is an estimated 50 species of mosquitoes in northern B.C. and 30 in the Yukon . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ invasive . <h> Places with the fewest mosquitoes <p> Weather and local geography influence mosquito activity , so you 're less likely to find them in drier and cooler climates , and windy cities tend to have decreased mosquito activity . <p> Higher elevations , cooler nights , and dry conditions in places like the Okanagan in B.C. , and Calgary and Canmore in Alberta reduce mosquito breeding . <p> Areas that experience coastal winds are likely to have fewer mosquitoes.
